paras: The attempted lynching of Bill Anderson was a threat by a mob at Tuskegee, Alabama, in July 1888 to lynch a 22-year-old Black prisoner held in the Macon County jail. Sheriff Pinkard took Anderson by train to the Montgomery jail before the mob acted, and the story circulated as a wire dispatch in papers from Atlanta to Kansas.

According to a dispatch from Montgomery, J. M. Knowles, described as "one of the most respectable citizens of Macon county," was awakened on the preceding Friday night by screams from the room of his two daughters. The dispatch said the elder daughter had found Anderson lying on the bed with her younger sister, and that he ran past Knowles and escaped. Anderson was caught, taken to Tuskegee, the county seat, on Monday, and jailed.

Threats of lynching followed, though at first "it was thought nothing serious was going to result." On the day of the dispatch, however, a mob began to form "with the avowed purpose of lynching the prisoner." Judging that the local military would be unable to protect him, Sheriff Pinkard hurried Anderson onto a train and lodged him that night in the Montgomery county jail "for safe keeping."

Anderson denied the charge and said he had not been in the vicinity, although the dispatch reported that both daughters identified him. No report of a trial or of Anderson's later fate appears in the coverage.

Every surviving account is a version of the same Montgomery dispatch, which treated the accusation as established and declared that the circumstantial evidence was so strong as to "preclude the possibility of an acquittal." The Wichita Eagle ran it on July 13 as "Dodging a Mob," and the Emporia Weekly News reprinted it under the same headline on July 19. The Atlanta Constitution printed it as a special dated July 11 under "The Scream of a Woman," with the subhead "Leads to the Arrest of an Offending Negro." The Western Kansas World, on July 21, headed it "A Negro Brute Narrowly Escapes Being Lynched."
None of the papers commented on the mob itself beyond reporting the sheriff's removal of the prisoner.
The versions differ on the daughters' ages: the Kansas papers said one was grown and one was 12, while the Atlanta Constitution gave their ages as nine and twelve.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Bill Anderson
bases: A mob formed at Tuskegee 'with the avowed purpose of lynching' a jailed prisoner, who was removed to Montgomery before it acted; a threatened lynching (A1, A2).
Anderson was not killed: the sheriff took him to the Montgomery jail before the mob acted (A1, A2). The mob's purpose was to punish an accused prisoner, but its size is not given.
All four papers print one dispatch from Montgomery in nearly identical words (A1, A2, A3, A4); no independent or local account was found.

accounts.label: Montgomery wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Anderson, identified by both Knowles daughters, was found on the younger daughter's bed, caught and jailed at Tuskegee; when a mob began forming to lynch him, the sheriff moved him to Montgomery.

accounts.label: Anderson's denial (as reported)
accounts.gist: Anderson 'stoutly declares his innocence' and said he was not in the vicinity at the time.

framing.detail: Kansas papers ran the dispatch as 'Dodging a Mob', presenting the accusation as fact and asserting that the evidence precluded acquittal.
The Atlanta Constitution headed the same text 'The Scream of a Woman / Leads to the Arrest of an Offending Negro in Montgomery'.
The Western Kansas World headed it 'A Negro Brute Narrowly Escapes Being Lynched', treating the accusation as proven while reporting the mob's failure.

conflicts.note: Same dispatch, differing in this phrase; neither version is better evidenced.
Both say the mob formed and the removal occurred 'today'.

Dispatch dated July 12 (A1) or July 11 (A2); mob formed 'today'

info: The mob formed and Anderson was removed to Montgomery on the day of the dispatch, dated July 12 in the Kansas papers and July 11 in the Atlanta Constitution; the alleged incident was on the preceding Friday and his arrest and jailing at Tuskegee on Monday.
Tuskegee, county seat of Macon county, where Anderson was jailed and the mob formed; the alleged incident was at the Knowles home in Macon county.
Bill Anderson, described as 'a negro' aged 22.
Accused of having been found lying on the bed with the younger daughter of J. M. Knowles in the daughters' room; he fled when the elder daughter screamed.
An unnamed mob at Tuskegee; no leaders or race given.
Anderson was confined in the Montgomery jail; no report of a trial or later fate was found.
